segments.text: Sociological research uses systematic methods to study social life. The goal is to move from assumptions and anecdotes toward evidence collected through transparent procedures.
This unit is highly practical. If you can design a small study in your mind, every concept becomes easier.

items.text: Scientific method
: The scientific approach involves clear questions, concepts, evidence, transparent methods, analysis and conclusions that can be scrutinized by others.
Steps in research

: A common sequence is: identify problem → review existing knowledge → formulate question/hypothesis where appropriate → define concepts/variables → choose design and sample → collect data → analyse → interpret → report.
Research design
: A research design is the overall plan for answering a question. Different questions require different designs; descriptive, comparative and explanatory aims should not be mixed carelessly.
Questionnaire
: Questionnaires collect standardized responses. Good questions are clear, neutral, relevant and ordered carefully. Closed questions are easier to quantify; open questions allow richer responses.
Survey
: A survey studies a sample to describe or analyse a population. Sampling is crucial: a large biased sample can still produce misleading results.
Observation
: Observation records behaviour or settings directly. It may be participant or non-participant, structured or less structured. Observer effects and ethical issues must be considered.
Case study
: A case study examines a person, group, organization, community or event in depth. It provides rich contextual understanding but may have limited generalizability.
Sampling

: Probability sampling gives known selection chances and is useful for population inference. Non-probability sampling may be useful in exploratory or hard-to-reach settings but has greater limits for generalization.
Ethics
: Researchers should protect participants through informed consent where applicable, privacy/confidentiality, minimization of harm and honesty about the study. Vulnerable groups require added care.
Correlation and causation
: If two variables are associated, one does not automatically cause the other. Causal claims require stronger evidence and attention to alternative explanations.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

blocks.text: From a social concern to a researchable question

segments.text: Research begins by narrowing a broad concern into a question that identifies the phenomenon, population, place and sometimes time period. 'Unemployment is a problem' is not yet a research question; 'How does long-term unemployment affect household decision-making among urban youth in a specified district?' is much closer to one.

items.text: Literature review
: Researchers examine existing studies to refine concepts, identify what is already known, avoid duplication and select appropriate methods.
Conceptualization
: Abstract ideas such as social class, trust or alienation must be defined clearly enough that readers know what is meant.
Operationalization
: Researchers decide how a concept will be observed or measured, for example through income bands, survey scales, interview themes or behavioural indicators.
Hypothesis
: A hypothesis is a testable expectation about variables. Exploratory qualitative research may begin with open questions instead of formal hypotheses.
Quantitative
: Uses numerical measurement and statistical analysis to estimate distributions, relationships or effects. Strengths include comparability and population inference when sampling is sound.
Qualitative
: Uses interviews, observation, documents and other rich data to understand meanings, processes and context. Strength is depth, not statistical representativeness.
Mixed methods

: Combines quantitative and qualitative evidence when a question benefits from both breadth and depth. Mixing methods is useful only when the components are integrated rather than placed side by side without purpose.
Method follows question
: No method is universally superior. A prevalence estimate, a causal test and an exploration of lived experience require different designs.
Question design
: Questions should be clear, neutral and limited to one idea. Double-barrelled questions, leading wording and vague time frames create measurement error.
Closed questions
: Fixed response categories are efficient for statistical comparison but can force respondents into options that do not fit.
Open questions
: Allow participants to express unexpected answers but require more complex coding and analysis.
Mode effects
: Face-to-face, telephone and online surveys differ in cost, coverage and social-desirability pressure.
Nonresponse
: If people who do not respond differ systematically from respondents, estimates can be biased even when the original sample was well designed.
Population and sample
: The population is the group about which the study seeks conclusions; the sample is the observed subset.
Simple random sampling
: Each element has a known chance of selection, reducing selection bias when the sampling frame is adequate.
Stratified sampling
: The population is divided into strata and sampled within each, often improving representation of important subgroups.
Cluster sampling
: Researchers sample naturally occurring clusters such as schools or neighbourhoods, which can reduce cost but requires analysis that accounts for clustering.
Convenience sampling
: Participants are selected because they are easy to reach. It may be useful for pilot or exploratory work but cannot support strong population generalization.
Purposive and snowball sampling
: Qualitative studies may deliberately select information-rich cases or use network referrals to reach hidden populations. The goal is depth or access, not statistical representativeness.
Participant observation
: The researcher joins or closely participates in a setting to understand practices from within. Access can reveal context unavailable in surveys but raises role and ethical challenges.
Non-participant observation
: The researcher observes without joining the activity to the same degree, which can reduce involvement but may limit understanding of meanings.
Reactivity
: People may alter behaviour because they know they are observed. Long-term field presence and unobtrusive measures can sometimes reduce this problem.
Field notes
: Systematic field notes distinguish direct observation from the researcher's interpretation. Reflexivity requires researchers to examine how their position affects access and interpretation.

blocks.text: Case studies, experiments and comparative designs

items.text: Case study
: Provides intensive analysis of a bounded case such as an organization, village, policy or movement. It is strong for mechanisms and context but weak for simple statistical generalization.
Experiment
: Random assignment and controlled manipulation can support causal inference, but many sociological questions cannot be ethically or practically randomized.
Natural/quasi-experiment
: Researchers use policy changes or naturally occurring contrasts to approximate causal comparison when randomization is unavailable. Validity depends on assumptions about comparability.
Comparative historical research

: Compares societies or periods using documents and historical evidence to explain institutional change. It is powerful for large-scale questions but depends on the quality and comparability of records.
Correlation
: Two variables are associated. This is evidence of a relationship, not proof of a causal path.
Reverse causation
: A may influence B, but B may also influence A. For example, social isolation can worsen health while poor health can also reduce social participation.
Confounding
: A third variable may influence both. Education can be associated with earnings partly because of skills, family background, networks and labour-market selection.
Causal mechanism
: A credible causal claim explains the process linking cause to outcome and tests alternative explanations using design and evidence.
Reliability
: A measure is reliable when it produces sufficiently consistent information under appropriate conditions. Reliability is necessary but does not prove that the intended concept is measured well.
Validity
: Validity asks whether evidence supports the interpretation made from the data. Content, construct and criterion-related evidence may all be relevant.
Informed consent
: Participants should usually understand the study and voluntarily agree, though some observational research requires special ethical justification when prior consent is impracticable.
Confidentiality
: Researchers must protect identifiable information and explain limits. Digital data can create new re-identification risks even when names are removed.
Minimization of harm
: Sensitive topics can create emotional, social or legal risks. Ethical design limits unnecessary exposure and provides safeguards.
Vulnerable populations

: Children, prisoners, displaced people and others with constrained autonomy require additional protection. Access from an authority figure does not automatically equal free consent from each participant.

segments.text: Statistical significance is not the same as substantive importance, and a large effect in one context may not generalize elsewhere. Qualitative depth is not the same as representativeness. Good research reports uncertainty, missing data, sampling limitations and plausible alternative explanations.

The final question is always whether the method supports the claim. A survey can estimate prevalence if sampling is sound; it usually cannot establish causation by itself. A case study can reveal mechanisms and context; it cannot by itself estimate how common those mechanisms are in a whole country.
Reading the flow: each step creates the conditions for the next; the arrows show sequence or influence, not inevitability unless the text explicitly says so.

items.text: Practise turning “unemployment” into a researchable question with a defined population and location.
Design a 10-question questionnaire and then identify biased/leading questions.
Make a methods table: survey, observation, case study → strengths → weaknesses → best use.
Always write sampling and ethics in research-method answers.

rows: Avoid this error Do not write that qualitative research is “unscientific.” Scientific quality depends on systematic, transparent and appropriate methods, whether data are qualitative, quantitative or mixed.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Explain the scientific method and research steps, then design, questionnaire/survey, observation and case study, followed by sampling, ethics and interpretation limits.
• Conerly, Holmes, & Tamang, Introduction to Sociology 3e (OpenStax, 2021).
• Standard research-design, sampling and ethics principles; claims of causation require designs capable of addressing confounding and alternative explanations.
• The research method must fit the research question.
• Sampling quality matters more than sample size alone.
• Ethics is part of research quality, not an optional extra.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
